title: Checks for usage of <integer>::max_value(), std::<integer>::MAX, std::<float>::EPSILON, etc.
summary: All of these have been superseded by the associated constants on their respective types, such as i128::MAX. These legacy items may be deprecated in a future version of rust. Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for items that implement .len() but not .is_empty().
summary: It is good custom to have both methods, because for some data structures, asking about the length will be a costly operation, whereas .is_empty() can usually answer in constant time. Also it used to lead to false positives on the len_zero lint – currently that lint will ignore such entities. Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for getting the length of something via .len() just to compare to zero, and suggests using .is_empty() where applicable.
summary: Some structures can answer .is_empty() much faster than calculating their length. So it is good to get into the habit of using .is_empty(), and having it is cheap. Besides, it makes the intent clearer than a manual comparison in some contexts. Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for let-bindings, which are subsequently returned.
summary: It is just extraneous code. Remove it to make your code more rusty. Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for let _ = <expr> where the resulting type of expr implements Future
summary: Futures must be polled for work to be done. The original intention was most likely to await the future and ignore the resulting value. Clippy puts this lint in the suspicious group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for let _ = sync_lock.
summary: This supports mutex and rwlock in parking_lot. For std locks see the rustc lint let_underscore_lock This statement immediately drops the lock instead of extending its lifetime to the end of the scope, which is often not intended. To extend lock lifetime to the end of the scope, use an underscore-prefixed name instead (i.e. _lock). If you want to explicitly drop the lock, std::mem::drop conveys your intention better and is less error-prone. Clippy puts this lint in the correctness group, at the level deny.

title: Checks for let _ = <expr> where expr is #[must_use]
summary: To ensure that all #[must_use] types are used rather than ignored. Clippy puts this lint in the restriction group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for let _ = <expr> without a type annotation, and suggests to either provide one, or remove the let keyword altogether.
summary: The let _ = <expr> expression ignores the value of <expr>, but will continue to do so even if the type were to change, thus potentially introducing subtle bugs. By supplying a type annotation, one will be forced to re-visit the decision to ignore the value in such cases. Clippy puts this lint in the restriction group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for binding a unit value.
summary: A unit value cannot usefully be used anywhere. So binding one is kind of pointless. Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Detects when a variable is declared with an explicit type of _.
summary: It adds noise, : _ provides zero clarity or utility. Clippy puts this lint in the complexity group, at the level warn.
